background.executionContext:
**Commands used** (all via the prescribed `./b4w.ps1`, scoped to a named session `-s eval-cookies` to avoid the documented default-session singleton collision):

`goto` · `cookie-set` ×7 · `cookie-list` ×8 · `cookie-get` · `cookie-delete` ×3 · `cookie-clear` ×4 · `localstorage-set/list/get/delete/clear` · `sessionstorage-set/list/get/delete/clear` · `state-save` · `state-load` · `eval` ×3

**Key decisions and workarounds:**

- **Named session.** The docs warn the unnamed default session is a singleton shared by every invocation; the scratch directory showed a concurrent run in progress, so I isolated with `-s eval-cookies`. This worked cleanly and required no extra setup.
- **The Git Bash `--path /` wall (the one real friction point).** `./b4w.ps1 cookie-set session_id abc123 --domain localhost --path /` failed immediately: Git Bash's MSYS path conversion rewrites a bare `/` argument to `C:/Program Files/Git/` *before* PowerShell starts. The CLI detected the rewrite and failed fast with an actionable message naming two fixes. I used the suggested `MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' ./b4w.ps1 ...` prefix to stay on the required invocation; I also independently confirmed `./b4w.sh` works for the same command.
- **Timestamp.** Rather than the `7d`/`1w` shorthand, I passed a computed RFC 3339 datetime (`2026-10-20T17:04:33Z`) to exercise the documented absolute-timestamp path; the confirmation line echoed `expires=1792515873`, exactly one week out.
- **State file location.** `browser_state.json` was written into the run's scratch directory (`.test-sessions/20261013T0154334271610Z/`) via a relative path, satisfying the temp-file rule while keeping the requested filename.
- **Extra state on the round-trip.** For step 14 I also set a localStorage marker, because `state-save` persists cookies *and* localStorage — restoring only a cookie would not have proven the round-trip. Both came back.
- **Cleanup.** Probe cookies (`eq_form_ok`, `via_sh`, `rel_week`, `other_site_cookie`, `sec_other`, `ho_check`) were cleared; the session, localStorage, and sessionStorage were left empty.

**What the CLI did notably well:** the whole 17-step flow needed **no manual server setup** (daemon + backend auto-started on first `goto`); help is genuinely task-oriented — `--help localstorage-set` contained the literal `'{"lang":"en","tz":"UTC"}'` example the task called for, and `--help cookie-set`'s example matched step 2 verbatim; error messages are consistently specific and name the fix (invalid `sameSite` says "case-sensitive; got 'lax'"; invalid `--expires` enumerates all three accepted formats); and `cookie-get --full` (discovered while checking whether the bare-value output was an inconsistency) turned out to be a documented escape hatch.

**Outcome:** 17/17 steps completed. One command required a retry (~94% first-attempt success, 100% final), and no step was blocked.

assessment.completionStatus: Successful - all 17 steps completed and independently verified at the browser level (real cookie jar, httpOnly honored, domain filter genuinely filtering, localStorage/sessionStorage cycles, and a full state-save/clear/state-load round-trip).
assessment.successRate: 100% of steps completed; ~94% succeeded on the first attempt (step 2's first attempt was rejected by Git Bash, then succeeded with the CLI's own documented workaround).
assessment.majorBlockers: None. The only first-attempt failure was the Git Bash / MSYS argv rewrite of the bare '--path /' argument. It was detected, never silently misapplied, and the CLI's error message supplied two working fixes; the task continued without loss.
assessment.mostConfusingAspects: The shell-integration seam is the only genuinely confusing area, and it is a Windows/Git-Bash artifact rather than a CLI design flaw. Two things compound it: (1) the top-level `help` never mentions Git Bash, MSYS, or the ./b4w.sh escape hatch, so a bash user meets the caveat only by colliding with it; and (2) the most natural workaround a user reaches for, the equals form --path=/, fails with a misleading error naming a value ('C') they never typed — strictly worse feedback than the bare-/ spelling it was meant to avoid. Everything else was unusually clear: the storage command family, the flag names (--domain/--path/--httpOnly/--secure/--sameSite/--expires), and the state-save/state-load split all behaved exactly as the help described.
assessment.mostValuableImprovements: 1) Surface the Git Bash caveat and the ./b4w.sh route in the top-level help output (cli/browser4-cli/src/help.rs), and note that --path defaults to '/' so the flag can simply be omitted from bash. 2) Extend the MSYS guard in b4w.ps1 to test the substring after the first '=' so the --name=value spelling gets the good error message instead of a misleading one. 3) Normalize the cookie JSON schema to a fixed key set (or document the optional keys) so automation can rely on it. All three are small, localized changes.

issues.title: Cookie path '/' is unusable via the documented ./b4w.ps1 invocation from Git Bash

sections.body:
./b4w.ps1 -s eval-cookies cookie-set session_id abc123 --domain localhost --path / --httpOnly --secure
(also: ./b4w.ps1 cookie-list --path /)
sections.label: Reproduction

sections.body: The cookie is stored with Path=/, matching the example in the tool's own help text. The documented, primary entry point for this repo (./b4w.ps1) should be able to express a documented flag value.
sections.label: Expected Behavior

sections.body: Exit 1 with: "Error: argument 'C:/Program Files/Git/' (probably typed as '/') was rewritten by Git Bash's MSYS path conversion before PowerShell started. The original value is unrecoverable..." The command only works if prefixed with MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' or run through a second wrapper, ./b4w.sh.
sections.label: Actual Behavior

sections.body: Git Bash's MSYS path conversion rewrites '/'-leading argv tokens when it spawns the native pwsh process, so the value is destroyed before either b4w.ps1 or the CLI runs; neither can recover it. b4w.ps1:86-144 correctly detects the mangled form and fails fast rather than proceeding with a wrong value, and the message names two working fixes — so the defect is not silent corruption but discoverability: the repo's prescribed invocation is the one that fails, and the 354-line top-level `help` output never mentions Git Bash or MSYS (verified by grep), nor does it mention ./b4w.sh. A bash user following `help` learns of the caveat only by hitting the wall; it appears solely in per-command help (cookie-set/cookie-delete) and in references/storage-state.md.
sections.label: Root Cause Analysis

sections.body: cli/browser4-cli/src/help.rs (top-level help text); b4w.ps1:86-144 (guard, correct as-is); cli/browser4-cli/src/commands.rs:2550,2487,2600 (option docs)
sections.label: Code Pointer

sections.body:
- Add a one-line 'Git Bash / MSYS users: invoke via ./b4w.sh' note to the top-level `help` output (cli/browser4-cli/src/help.rs), which currently mentions neither Git Bash nor MSYS.
- Document the zero-workaround path in the same note: --path defaults to '/', so bash users can simply omit the flag (`cookie-set session_id abc123 --domain localhost --httpOnly --secure`).
- Where repo/agent instructions prescribe ./b4w.ps1 for bash shells, prescribe ./b4w.sh instead (CLAUDE.md already documents both, but the distinction is buried).
- Keep the existing guard and message unchanged — they are exemplary; only the surfaces that lead the user to it need to change.

issues.title: Equals-form --path=/ bypasses the MSYS guard and yields a misleading error naming a value the user never typed

sections.body:
./b4w.ps1 -s eval-cookies cookie-set eq_form v1 --domain localhost --path=/
Then confirm the same command succeeds with conversion disabled:
MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' ./b4w.ps1 -s eval-cookies cookie-set eq_form_ok v1 --domain localhost --path=/
sections.label: Reproduction

sections.body: Either the cookie is set with Path=/, or the user gets the same clear MSYS-rewrite guidance that the bare `--path /` spelling produces.
sections.label: Expected Behavior

sections.body: Exit 1 with: "Error: option '--path' was rejected: 'C' is not a valid cookie path (must start with '/')". The message names the value 'C' — a string the user never typed — and gives no indication that Git Bash rewrote the argument. The `--option=` spelling is exactly what a user tries after learning that a bare `/` is unsafe, so this is the likely second encounter.
sections.label: Actual Behavior

sections.body: MSYS rewrites the portion after '=' , so '--path=/' arrives as '--path=C:/Program Files/Git/'. The guard in b4w.ps1:123-131 compares each whole argv token against the MSYS root: $ArgIsRoot tests equality with the root and $ArgUnderRoot tests a StartsWith($RootFwd + '/') prefix. A token retaining its '--path=' prefix matches neither, so it is forwarded; the mangled string is subsequently split (on the space in 'C:/Program Files/Git/' and/or the ':' separator) somewhere between pwsh and the CLI, leaving handle_cookie_set's validation (main.rs:6202) to receive the literal 'C'. The guard's comment explicitly reasons about equality vs. prefix for the standalone-'/' case but does not consider embedded name=value forms. (The exact point at which the mangled token is truncated to 'C' was not isolated; the guard's non-firing for this spelling is directly proven by the absence of its message.)
sections.label: Root Cause Analysis

sections.body:
- In the guard loop, when a token fails the as-is comparison, retry the root comparison against the substring after the first '=' — this covers `--path=`, and also `--selector=`, `--sql=`, `--domain=`, and every other `--name=value` flag.
- Generalize the detection to the signature of a mangled value: a token matching `^--?[A-Za-z][A-Za-z-]*=<drive>:/` caught under $env:MSYSTEM should emit the same friendly guidance.
- As a backstop, have path-rooted option-validation errors append the Git Bash hint when $env:MSYSTEM is set, so any future spelling that slips the guard still explains itself.
- Add a regression test for the `--path=/` spelling next to the existing bare-`/` case in the b4w.ps1 guard tests.

issues.title: cookie-list and state-save omit absent cookie attributes instead of emitting nulls

sections.body:
./b4w.ps1 -s eval-cookies cookie-set session_id abc123 --domain localhost --path / --httpOnly --secure
./b4w.ps1 -s eval-cookies cookie-set theme dark --sameSite Lax --expires 7d
./b4w.ps1 -s eval-cookies cookie-list
sections.label: Reproduction

sections.body: A stable schema per cookie object, with every attribute present (null where absent) — as the cookie example in references/storage-state.md suggests, showing name/value/domain/path/expires/httpOnly/secure/sameSite together.
sections.label: Expected Behavior

sections.body: The session_id object contains no `expires` and no `sameSite` key at all, while the theme object contains both; httpOnly/secure are always present. Consumers must branch on key presence, and `cookie.expires` reads as undefined rather than null. The same omission appears in the state-save file (test_cookie was written without expires/sameSite), so the two JSON surfaces at least agree with each other.
sections.label: Actual Behavior

sections.body: The cookie-to-JSON mapping skips fields that the underlying cookie struct reports as absent (session cookies have no expiry; unspecified SameSite has no value) rather than normalizing them to null. This is faithful to CDP's cookie representation but makes the CLI's own JSON an optional-key schema. Impact is confined to typed/schema-validated consumers — jq and similar tools are unaffected.
sections.label: Root Cause Analysis

sections.body: cli/browser4-cli/src/main.rs (cookie-to-JSON mapping shared by handle_cookie_list and the state-save writer)
sections.label: Code Pointer

sections.body:
- Emit a fixed key set per cookie (name, value, domain, path, expires, httpOnly, secure, sameSite) with null for absent values, so the schema is stable and self-describing.
- If the omission is deliberate CDP fidelity, state it explicitly in `--help cookie-list` and in the state-save file-format section of references/storage-state.md — the current help says only 'Output is always JSON (an array of cookie objects)'.
- Low priority: no task step was impeded, and exit codes and values were correct throughout.
